keyFacts: Germany was unified in 1871 under Prussian leadership and Wilhelm I became the first Kaiser.
The Kaiser controlled the armed forces and appointed the Chancellor and government ministers.
The Reichstag was elected by adult men over 25, while the Bundesrat represented the German states.
The Kaiser could ignore Reichstag advice and dissolve it, limiting parliamentary power.
Industrialisation made Germany a major producer of iron and steel by 1913.
Rapid urban growth created overcrowding, poor housing and difficult working conditions for many workers.
The SPD demanded political and social reform and became the largest Reichstag party in 1912.
Industrial growth strengthened Germany but also increased social and political tensions.
Weltpolitik aimed to increase Germany's international power and influence.
Navy Laws between 1898 and 1912 expanded the fleet and helped trigger rivalry with Britain.
Naval expansion was expensive and contributed to government debt and taxation pressures.
The First World War caused severe food shortages, inflation and falling living standards in Germany.
The Allied blockade reduced imports and contributed to malnutrition and civilian hardship.
By autumn 1918 Germany faced military defeat, mutiny and political unrest.
The armistice ended fighting on 11 November 1918 after the Kaiser's abdication.
The Weimar Republic began in 1919 with an elected President, Chancellor, Reichstag and proportional representation.
Proportional representation widened representation but often produced coalition governments.
The Treaty of Versailles imposed territorial losses, military restrictions and reparations on Germany.
The Spartacist uprising challenged the new republic from the left in January 1919.
The Kapp Putsch challenged it from the right in March 1920 and failed after a general strike.
In 1923 occupation of the Ruhr and passive resistance helped trigger hyperinflation.
Stresemann ended passive resistance in the Ruhr and introduced a new currency to stabilise Germany.
The Dawes Plan brought American loans and made reparations payments more manageable.
The Young Plan reduced the annual burden and extended the payment period, but reparations continued.
Stresemann's foreign policy improved Germany's international position through Locarno and League of Nations membership.
Recovery remained vulnerable because German prosperity relied heavily on US credit.
After 1929 US loans were withdrawn and unemployment rose to about six million by 1932.
The Depression weakened confidence in coalition government and increased support for extremist parties.
Nazi propaganda was adapted to different audiences and promised work, order, national revival and opposition to communism.
Hitler's speaking, modern campaigning and the SA helped the Nazis build support, although SA violence also alarmed voters.
The Nazis won 230 Reichstag seats in July 1932 but fell to 196 in November 1932.
Hindenburg initially resisted appointing Hitler Chancellor.
Papen and other conservatives believed they could control Hitler inside a cabinet dominated by non-Nazis.
Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933 through appointment rather than a direct popular vote.
The Reichstag Fire Decree removed key civil liberties and made it easier to arrest communist and other opponents.
The Enabling Act allowed Hitler's government to legislate without normal parliamentary approval.
The Nazis dismantled trade unions, opposition parties and independent political organisations during 1933.
The Night of the Long Knives removed Röhm and leading SA figures and reassured the army.
After Hindenburg died in August 1934 the army swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler.
Goebbels coordinated Nazi propaganda through newspapers, radio, cinema, rallies, posters and cultural organisations.
Cheap radios and public loudspeakers helped spread Nazi messages to a mass audience.
Censorship restricted hostile newspapers, books, music, theatre and art.
The SS, Gestapo, police, courts and concentration camps created overlapping systems of surveillance and repression.
The Gestapo depended substantially on denunciations rather than having enough officers to watch everyone.
The first concentration camp at Dachau opened in 1933, initially holding many political opponents.

triggers: nazis controlled germany only through propaganda
misconceptions.correction: Propaganda was important, but Nazi control also relied on censorship, the SS, Gestapo, courts, concentration camps and the removal of political opposition.

keyFacts: The National Labour Service (RAD) put young men into compulsory work schemes and later became part of preparations for war.
Public works, rearmament and conscription all contributed to the fall in recorded unemployment.
Schacht's New Plan controlled imports and promoted trade arrangements to conserve foreign currency.
From 1936 Göring's Four Year Plan prioritised rearmament and self-sufficiency in preparation for war.
Synthetic substitutes and domestic production were encouraged to reduce dependence on imported raw materials.
Workers lost free trade unions and strikes but were offered schemes such as Strength Through Joy.
Nazi policy initially encouraged women to marry, have children and focus on family life.
Marriage loans and awards for large families were used to encourage births, while policy changed as wartime labour needs grew.
Education was reshaped around Nazi ideas: textbooks and curricula stressed race, nationalism, obedience and physical fitness.
Membership of Nazi youth organisations expanded rapidly and became compulsory in 1939.
The Hitler Youth prepared boys for military roles while the League of German Maidens emphasised fitness, domestic skills and motherhood.
The Nazis signed a Concordat with the Catholic Church in 1933 but relations later deteriorated.
The Confessing Church opposed Nazi attempts to dominate Protestant Christianity.

triggers: all german young people supported hitler youth
misconceptions.correction: Hitler Youth membership became compulsory, but some young Germans resisted or joined alternative groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth.

keyFacts: Nazi racial policy persecuted Jews and other groups the regime labelled racially or socially undesirable.
The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 removed German citizenship from Jews and prohibited marriage between Jews and non-Jewish Germans.
Kristallnacht in November 1938 involved widespread attacks on Jewish homes, businesses and synagogues and mass arrests.
Other victims included Roma and Sinti people, disabled people, homosexual men and Jehovah's Witnesses.
During the war persecution escalated into deportation, ghettos, mass shootings and systematic mass murder.
Opposition ranged from private non-compliance to organised resistance and assassination attempts.
Swing Youth rejected Nazi cultural conformity and listened to jazz and swing music.
The Edelweiss Pirates rejected Hitler Youth regimentation; some groups later undertook more active resistance.
The White Rose, including Hans and Sophie Scholl, distributed anti-Nazi leaflets before members were arrested and executed in 1943.
Church figures including Martin Niemöller and Dietrich Bonhoeffer opposed aspects of Nazi rule.
On 20 July 1944 Claus von Stauffenberg planted a bomb intended to kill Hitler; Hitler survived and the conspirators were punished.
